newsitem.title: USA: Calif. cuts length of power-purchase contracts.
newsitem.headline: Calif. cuts length of power-purchase contracts.

text.p: The California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) has cut the length of new power-purchase contracts required of investor-owned utilities to five years, the commission said Wednesday.
As a result, "the impact on competitive transition costs is eliminated," it said. Under California state legislation, electricity will be sold at market rates by 2002.
In the past, utilities were required to enter into 30-year deals with independent power producers, also known as "qualifying facilities" (QF).
The decision stipulates that terms of contracts set before April 16, 1996, still stand.

The state's three major investor-owned utilities--Pacific Gas and Electric Co, Edison International's Southern California Edison Co and Enova Corp's San Diego Gas and Electric Co--argued that the mandated contracts result in above-market costs.
As the electricity industry moves away from a system of regulated monopolies toward open competition, the utilities say the QF contracts make it harder for them to compete.
The utilties had sought to limit new QF contracts to one year, but the CPUC decided the independent power producers needed more time to recoup their investments.
